keyframes.prompt: Vertical 2:3 macro photo looking straight into a honeybee comb inside a hive. Clean golden-yellow beeswax hexagonal cells fill the whole frame, seen almost straight on and slightly from above, so the inner walls and the bottom of each cell are visible. One cell sits exactly in the center of the frame and is about one quarter of the frame width. At the bottom of the central cell, one tiny white honeybee egg stands upright, shaped like a small curved grain of rice. All the other cells are empty and clean. No bees. Warm soft light, sharp focus on the central cell, the cells near the edges slightly out of focus. Keep everything important away from the left and right edges. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the honeycomb, every cell, the lighting and the camera angle exactly the same. The egg in the central cell is gone. One tiny glossy white honeybee larva, curled in a C shape, lies at the bottom of the central cell in a small pool of milky white royal jelly. All the other cells stay empty.

Edit this image. Keep the honeycomb, every cell, the lighting and the camera angle exactly the same. The larva in the central cell is now large and plump, glossy pearly white with fine ring segments, curled in a thick C shape that fills the bottom of the cell. Only one larva. All the other cells stay empty.

Edit this image. Keep the honeycomb, every cell, the lighting and the camera angle exactly the same. The central cell is now sealed with a slightly domed, light brown, porous wax cap that covers the whole opening of the cell. The larva is no longer visible. All the other cells stay empty and open.

Edit this image. Keep the honeycomb, every cell, the lighting and the camera angle exactly the same. The wax cap of the central cell now has a ragged round hole in the middle. The head of one young honeybee pokes out of the hole, facing the camera: two large black compound eyes, two bent antennae, small mandibles and pale fuzzy hair. A few wax crumbs lie on the rim of the cell. All the other cells stay empty.

Edit this image. Keep the honeycomb, every cell, the lighting and the camera angle exactly the same. The young honeybee has fully climbed out. The central cell is now open and empty, with ragged bits of the wax cap left on its rim. The bee stands still on the comb directly below the central cell, seen from above, head pointing toward the bottom of the frame, the tip of its abdomen at the lower rim of the central cell. It has a fuzzy golden-brown thorax, a black and golden striped abdomen, folded clear wings and six legs. The bee is about half the frame width long. Only one bee.

clips.prompt: Static locked-off camera, no camera movement, no zoom. Time-lapse. The egg in the central cell slowly hatches into a tiny white larva lying in milky royal jelly. The other cells stay empty. Nothing else changes.

Static locked-off camera, no camera movement, no zoom. Time-lapse. The white larva slowly grows bigger and bigger until it fills the bottom of the cell. The other cells stay empty. Nothing else changes.

Static locked-off camera, no camera movement, no zoom. Time-lapse. A light brown wax cap slowly grows inward from the rim of the central cell until it seals the cell. The other cells stay empty. Nothing else changes.

Static locked-off camera, no camera movement, no zoom. Time-lapse. A young bee slowly chews a hole through the wax cap from inside and pushes its head out. The other cells stay empty. Nothing else changes.
Static locked-off camera, no camera movement, no zoom. The young bee slowly climbs out of the cell onto the comb, then stands still. The other cells stay empty. Nothing else changes.
